Plotting group-specific smooths and parametric interactions

Source: vignettes/articles/smooth-effects.Rmd
smooth-effects.Rmd

Effect plots show how one smooth or parametric term contributes to the linear predictor. To obtain the expected response in these examples, add the model terms and intercept, then apply the inverse link. In the log-link model below, that means exponentiating the sum to get mean carbon dioxide uptake. We use the plant experiment from Working with glmmTMB models in gratia to plot curves for individual plants, then use daily air quality measurements to plot interactions between continuous and categorical predictors.

Load {gratia}, {mgcv} and {ggplot2} for the examples.

library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")

Fit and plot plant-specific smooth curves

The carbon dioxide experiment measured uptake at seven concentrations on each of twelve plants, with three plants per combination of origin and treatment. The Gamma model with a log link keeps the fitted means positive and lets the spread increase with the mean. In the model below, s(log_conc) allows the shared uptake curve to level off as concentration increases. The t2() term combines a spline for concentration with a plant random effect so that each plant can have its own smooth departure from the shared curve.

plant <- as.data.frame(CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)
plant$log_conc <- log(plant$conc) - mean(log(plant$conc))
plant_gam <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log_conc, k = 5) +
    t2(log_conc, Plant, bs = c("cr", "re"), k = c(4, 12), full = TRUE),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML")
overview(plant_gam)
#> 
#> Generalized Additive Model with 6 terms
#> 
#>   term                             type        k   edf ref.edf statistic p.value
#>   <chr>                            <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 Intercept                        parame…    NA  1       1        52.7  < 0.001
#> 2 TypeMississippi                  parame…    NA  1       1        -3.31 0.00181
#> 3 Treatmentchilled                 parame…    NA  1       1        -1.26 0.21419
#> 4 TypeMississippi:Treatmentchilled parame…    NA  1       1        -2.57 0.01349
#> 5 s(log_conc)                      TPRS        4  3.85    3.96     79.2  < 0.001
#> 6 t2(log_conc,Plant)               Tensor…    48 30.3    43         8.76 < 0.001

The penalties pull plant-specific departures towards zero. With full = TRUE, the model can penalise different parts of the tensor product separately. The concentration basis is small because there are only seven observations per plant. Use re_levels to plot the departures for three named plants from the nonchilled Quebec group.

smooths(plant_gam)
#> [1] "s(log_conc)"        "t2(log_conc,Plant)"
draw(plant_gam, select = "t2(log_conc,Plant)",
  re_levels = list(Plant = c("Qn1", "Qn2", "Qn3")),
  xlab = "Centred log concentration", ylab = "Plant contribution to log uptake") &
  theme(legend.position = "right") & labs(colour = "Plant")

The concentration goes on the horizontal axis even if the plant factor comes first in the tensor formula. re_levels selects which plants to display and keeps their order from the fitted factor. To see the fitted mean for each plant, plot the fitted values against the observations. These values combine the shared curve, the plant’s departure, the intercept and the terms for origin and treatment before applying the inverse link. The concentration units are microlitres per litre (\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}), as reported in Table 1 of the original study.

plant$mean_uptake <- fitted(plant_gam)
ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, group = Plant, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_uptake)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = expression(CO[2] ~ concentration ~ (mu * L ~ L^{-1})),
    y = expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1})))

The fitted curves rise rapidly and then flatten for these plants. They include each plant’s estimated departure. At the group level, the model assumes the same concentration response shape for all combinations of origin and treatment, with group differences entering as multipliers of mean uptake. Use variance_comp() to extract the variance components for the penalties on the shared smooth and the plant-specific departures.

variance_comp(plant_gam)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   .component           .variance .std_dev .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>   <chr>                    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 s(log_conc)           0.320      0.566    0.248      1.29  
#> 2 t2(log_conc,Plant)rr  0.000106   0.0103   0.00640    0.0165
#> 3 t2(log_conc,Plant)1r  0.000957   0.0309   0.0186     0.0515
#> 4 t2(log_conc,Plant)2r  0.000502   0.0224   0.0141     0.0355
#> 5 scale                 0.00346    0.0588   0.0471     0.0734

The spline rows describe how strongly the model penalises different parts of the fitted curves. The scale row estimates the Gamma dispersion. Multiplying it by the squared fitted mean gives the estimated variance of uptake around that mean.

Fit temperature, wind and month interactions

The airquality data contain daily New York measurements from May to September 1973. Ozone is in parts per billion, temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, wind speed in miles per hour, and solar radiation in Langleys; see ?datasets::airquality for the sources. We retain complete cases, so our analysis uses the days with all needed measurements.

The question is whether ozone’s association with temperature depends on wind, and whether that relationship is stable across summer months. We model log ozone with a Gaussian distribution, allow a smooth association with solar radiation, and use a temperature-by-wind-by-month interaction.

ozone <- na.omit(airquality[c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp", "Month")])
ozone$month <- factor(ozone$Month, labels = month.abb[5:9])
contrasts(ozone$month) <- contr.treatment(levels(ozone$month))
ozone_gam <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R, k = 6) + Temp * Wind * month,
  data = ozone, method = "REML")
table(ozone$month)
#> 
#> May Jun Jul Aug Sep 
#>  24   9  26  23  29
overview(ozone_gam)
#> 
#> Generalized Additive Model with 21 terms
#> 
#>    term          type           k   edf ref.edf statistic p.value
#>    <chr>         <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>  
#>  1 Intercept     parametric    NA     1       1     -2.56 0.01214
#>  2 Temp          parametric    NA     1       1      3.64 < 0.001
#>  3 Wind          parametric    NA     1       1      2.50 0.01423
#>  4 monthJun      parametric    NA     1       1      1.99 0.04966
#>  5 monthJul      parametric    NA     1       1      2.31 0.02322
#>  6 monthAug      parametric    NA     1       1      2.88 0.00501
#>  7 monthSep      parametric    NA     1       1      1.40 0.16547
#>  8 Temp:Wind     parametric    NA     1       1     -2.64 0.00975
#>  9 Temp:monthJun parametric    NA     1       1     -2.18 0.03153
#> 10 Temp:monthJul parametric    NA     1       1     -2.41 0.01808
#> # ℹ 11 more rows

A three-way interaction gives each month its own temperature-by-wind surface. Estimates can be imprecise where a month has few observations at similar temperatures and wind speeds. Plot those observations before interpreting the fitted surfaces.

ggplot(ozone, aes(Temp, Wind, colour = Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)",
    colour = "Ozone (ppb)")

Plot the separate interaction contributions

Start with the temperature-by-wind interaction for May, the reference month. parametric_terms() lists the available terms; parametric_effects() evaluates the chosen contribution on a grid for plotting.

parametric_terms(ozone_gam)
#>              Temp              Wind             month         Temp:Wind 
#>            "Temp"            "Wind"           "month"       "Temp:Wind" 
#>        Temp:month        Wind:month   Temp:Wind:month 
#>      "Temp:month"      "Wind:month" "Temp:Wind:month"
weather_effect <- parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind", n_2d = 30)
draw(weather_effect, surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")

Each point on the surface shows the fitted coefficient for Temp:Wind multiplied by the temperature and wind speed. The colours show how much this term adds to or subtracts from fitted log ozone. This is the interaction for May and the starting point for the other months’ interactions.

surface = "tile" uses vector rectangles, which can be useful in a vector figure. The default "raster" keeps large plots compact. n_2d = 30 evaluates 30 points along each surface axis. Increase n_2d for a finer display of the same fitted surface. Next plot how each month’s temperature-by-wind interaction differs from May’s.

draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind:month", n_2d = 25),
  surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")

The model uses treatment contrasts with May as the reference month, so the adjustment is zero in May. The panels share a colour scale centred at zero. dist controls how far a grid point can be from the observations before it is hidden, after scaling the two axes to range from zero to one. This uses observations from all months. Use the monthly scatterplots above to see which parts of each surface are supported by observations from that month.

Plot the temperature-by-month interaction to see how it adjusts the main temperature slope. Each month has its own straight line because the term is linear in temperature.

draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:month")) &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Additional contribution to log ozone")

These slopes must be combined with the reference temperature slope and the wind interactions to describe the model’s temperature association. The conditional comparisons article shows how to compare complete fitted values without isolating contrast-coded terms.

For a direct view of the complete model, predict at observed weather conditions:

ozone$fitted_log <- fitted(ozone_gam)
ggplot(ozone, aes(log(Ozone), fitted_log, colour = month)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Observed log ozone", y = "Fitted log ozone", colour = "Month")

The plot shows how closely the fitted mean log ozone follows the observed log concentrations. Under this model, exponentiating the fitted values gives the conditional median ozone concentration. To calculate the conditional arithmetic mean on the original scale, also account for the residual variance on the log scale. Similar residuals on nearby days could affect the uncertainty in monthly comparisons, so check residuals against the observation dates.

Show an interaction surface in three dimensions

The optional {ggcube} package can show the same numerical surface in three dimensions:

if (requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)) {
  draw(weather_effect, surface = "3d",
    surface_3d = list(yaw = 35, persp = FALSE)) &
    labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
}

Height and fill both represent the same partial contribution. Use the flat plots with their common colour scale to compare surfaces across months.

Parametric effect plots use the model’s covariate scale by default. For example, a term involving log(x) uses log(x) on the horizontal axis. back_transform = TRUE displays original covariate coordinates without changing effect values or intervals. With saved smooth estimates, prepare them using smooth_estimates(model, back_transform = TRUE) before asking draw() to use that scale. See the article on transformed covariates for worked examples, including transformations without an analytic inverse.

By default, the intervals include uncertainty in the intercept and its covariance with the plotted term. Set overall_uncertainty = FALSE for intervals that reflect uncertainty in the term alone. An interval for the difference between two predictions needs to account for their covariance.
